templates.scenario: During a busy stretch at {workplace|a}, {coworker} says in front of others, "You always leave your area a mess." You think your area was fine, and you feel your face getting hot. Later, things are calm and {coworker} is nearby.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Ask {coworker} privately what {coworker} noticed, share your side calmly, and agree on how to handle it next time.
options.why: A calm private conversation lets both of you explain what you saw and settle on a fix, and it avoids turning one comment into a bigger problem.

options.text: Go straight to your {lead} and ask for a ruling on whose version of the story is right this time.
options.why: Skipping the direct conversation makes a small disagreement bigger and leaves you and {coworker} no closer to working well together. A supervisor is for problems you cannot settle yourselves.
options.misconception: Going to the supervisor first is the strongest way to win.

options.text: Apologize and take the blame so the tension ends, even though you think your area was fine.
options.why: Giving in ends the moment but not the cause. The disagreement stays unresolved, and you may be asked to fix a problem you do not understand.
options.misconception: Giving in is the fastest way to end a conflict.

options.text: Avoid {coworker} and stay out of any shared tasks so there is no chance of another argument.
options.why: Avoiding the person lets the misunderstanding grow and makes teamwork harder. Working together means sorting out disagreements directly.
options.misconception: Avoiding the person solves the problem.

templates.principle: Handle disagreements directly and respectfully first: ask for the other person's view, share yours calmly, and agree on a fix. Bring in a supervisor when talking does not work or the issue is serious.

review.notes: Public, non-serious criticism; no harassment or safety element that would require escalation. Calm timing stated.

templates.scenario: On a shared project at {workplace|the}, {coworker} likes to talk through every step as a group before starting. You prefer to begin working on your own and check in later. You both want the project finished on time, and tension is starting to build.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Suggest a plan that uses both styles, such as a short planning huddle followed by independent work.
options.why: Both of you want the same result, so a plan that respects each person's working style resolves the tension without anyone having to lose.

options.text: Work in your own way and let the finished results show whose approach was better.
options.why: Turning a difference in style into a contest damages the working relationship, and a good result will not prove that the other approach was wrong.
options.misconception: The best way to settle a disagreement is to prove I am right.

options.text: Agree to do everything the way {coworker} prefers so the two of you stop disagreeing.
options.why: Giving in ends the argument but may leave you frustrated and less effective. A compromise lets both people do their best work.
options.misconception: Giving in completely is the fastest way to end tension.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to divide the project into separate parts so the two of you never need to coordinate.
options.why: Splitting the work to avoid each other removes the chance to work well together, and many projects need coordination. A blended approach is simpler.
options.misconception: Avoiding the other person is the best way to prevent conflict.

templates.principle: When styles differ but goals match, look for a plan that uses the strengths of both instead of winning, giving in or avoiding each other.

review.notes: Shared goal is stated; no policy content.

templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, {coworker} has left {coworker.poss} assigned part of {task|the} undone three times, and you have covered it twice. You spoke privately with {coworker} after the second time, and it happened again today. Your {lead} does not know about any of this.
templates.prompt: What is the best next step?

options.text: Calmly describe the pattern to your {lead}, with dates and examples, and ask for help setting clear duties.
options.why: A private conversation has already been tried and the problem continued, so it is now a pattern that your {lead} needs to know about. Specific examples make it easier to resolve fairly.

options.text: Talk privately with {coworker} one more time before involving anyone else.
options.why: Speaking directly is a good habit, but you have already done it once and the pattern continued. Waiting longer means more cover-ups and leaves your {lead} unaware.
options.misconception: One more conversation will fix it.

options.text: Keep covering the missing work quietly so the team does not fall behind and nobody gets upset.
options.why: Covering silently hides the problem from the person who can fix it, and it will keep happening while you carry the extra work.
options.misconception: Keeping the peace means staying quiet about a problem.

options.text: Do only your own part from now on and let the rest go undone, so {coworker} learns a lesson.
options.why: Letting work fail to teach a lesson hurts the team and the people relying on it, and it turns a work problem into a personal one.
options.misconception: Letting someone fail is a fair way to teach them.

templates.principle: When a direct conversation has not stopped a repeated problem, bring specific examples to the person who can help set expectations.

review.notes: Pattern and prior attempt stated; no harassment or safety content.

templates.timing: One private attempt has failed, so the first move now is escalation with specifics.

templates.scenario: After a disagreement about the schedule, a coworker writes this message to {coworker}. The writer wants to settle things.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that makes the conflict worse.

segments.whyFine: A greeting is a normal way to start.

segments.text: I wanted to follow up on yesterday's disagreement about the schedule.
segments.whyFine: Naming the topic calmly and directly is a good way to begin.

segments.text: You always do this, and you obviously never think about anyone else.
segments.why: Words like "always" and "never" attack the person instead of describing the problem, which makes the other person defensive.

segments.text: Could we talk for ten minutes tomorrow and work out a plan?
segments.whyFine: Asking for a short conversation to find a plan is constructive.

templates.principle: Describe the specific problem and invite a solution; sweeping accusations like 'always' and 'never' make people defensive.

review.notes: Only one line attacks the person.

templates.scenario: You had a tense disagreement with {coworker} at {workplace|the}, and you want to resolve it.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Take a moment to calm down and choose a private time to talk
Explain the specific issue calmly and listen to {coworker}'s view
Agree together on what each of you will do next
Check in later to see whether the plan is working

precedence.why: A calm, private conversation goes better than one held while upset.
You can only agree on a plan after both views have been heard.
You can only check a plan after it has been made.

templates.principle: Resolve conflicts in order: cool down, talk privately, agree on a plan, and follow up.
